title: Workflows
markdown:
Workflows are deterministic, multi-step orchestrations. The built-ins are registered in `openexecutive.workflows.WORKFLOW_REGISTRY`; user-created (dynamic) workflows are stored as data (see below). Each follows the same contract: structured input feeds an ordered list of named steps that render a Markdown artifact, persisted via `complete_run` into `workflow_runs.artifact`. Every step emits a `WorkflowEvent` (start/progress/complete) streamed over SSE at `/workflows/{name}/runs`.

The registry holds 24 built-in workflows, plus any number of user-created ones. Representative built-ins:

- `board_prep`, `quarterly_plan`, `annual_plan` — planning and governance deliverables.
- `performance_review`, `comp_refresh`, `org_design`, `exec_search_brief` — people and org artifacts (the last is an advisory hiring brief / scorecard from the CHRO, kept when the recruiting pipeline was removed).
- `crisis_comms`, `churn_deep_dive`, `competitive_teardown` — situational analyses.
- `department_check_in` — runs on department cadence; its `goal_status` step returns structured verdicts persisted back to `department_goals.status`.

### Change-aware principal briefs

`morning_brief` and `end_of_day_digest` are the two recurring briefs the scheduler DMs to the principal. Both are now a *delta*, not a re-list: the window is "since the last **delivered** brief" (`briefing.brief_state.since_for`; 24 h on a cold store, clamped to 7 days), activity comes from `_build_activity(limit, since=…)`, proposals (action category only) split into *new since last brief* — enumerated, with each item's why-now and next move — versus a one-line carried-over count, a *rewritten* block lists carried items the review rewrote inside the window (`brief_state.rewritten_since`: verdict `changed`, still open — the brief reports them under "what changed", never as done), and a *handled overnight* block lists what the Executive's alert review **completed** on its own (`brief_state.handled_since`; the `changed` verdict is excluded because the alert is still open). Section order: top call → what changed → handled overnight → needs you (new only) → waiting on → at risk. A date-free fingerprint of the inputs is compared to the last delivered one; if unchanged the artifact is the one-liner "Nothing new since yesterday's brief — N items still waiting on you." and no model call is made (`PRINCIPAL_BRIEF_SUPPRESS_UNCHANGED`; `force_full=true` on a manual run bypasses it). The workflow yields a `result` event with the fingerprint; only the scheduler records it, after a successful delivery, in `briefing_narrative` under scope `brief:<kind>` — so manual runs never advance the window.

Neither the nightly reflection nor the research synthesis can call `ack_alert`: both run unattended with open alerts rendered into their context, and those headlines are minted from inbound mail and chat, so an injected "the principal already dismissed 13" would be acted on with nobody watching. Closing an alert is the alert review's job, with evidence.

`executive_reflection` now carries memory: yesterday's standup (the previous completed run's artifact) is rendered into the context and the prompt forbids re-acting on anything listed there unless it changed; open alerts render with their id, review verdict and recommended move. Reflection never closes alerts — the alert review does, with evidence. It also renders an **OPEN LOOPS** block (up to 10, soonest due first, overdue flagged) from Attunement so the standup can connect a slipped promise to the rest of the org state; the nudge engine already chases overdue loops, so the prompt tells it not to DM about a loop merely for being overdue. A **WHAT LANDS** block (from the Attunement outcome ledger) shows, per person, how often each kind of proactive DM got answered over 30 days; the prompt steers DMs toward kinds that land and away from kinds a person reliably ignores. Reflection and research tag their tool execution as proactive (`tag_proactive`) so their DMs are counted. Resolving a wait-for-human approval (`resumer.apply_resolution`) marks the nudges that chased it `acted`. `close_open_loop` is withheld from reflection for the same reason as `ack_alert`: loop text is quoted from what people wrote.

### Wait-for-human pause

`wait_for_human` (`openexecutive/workflows/wait_for_human.py`) is a first-class step primitive that pauses a run: the runner calls `save_checkpoint`, the `workflow_runs` row moves to `status='awaiting_human'`, and the serialized `WaitForHumanEvent` is stored in `state_json`. (Department authority is a *separate* mechanism — `propose_only` departments file a briefing alert via `departments.authority.propose_via_alert` and mark the scheduled action done; they do not route through this gate.)

**Delivery.** Both checkpoint sites — the SSE route and the `run_workflow` chat tool — call `workflows.gate_delivery.deliver_gate_question` immediately *before* checkpointing, so `state_json` carries the routing fields a reply is matched against. Two modes. When the approver is the person already in the conversation (the chat session's `origin_channel` is set and its `caller_person_id` is the gate's `person_id`), nothing is sent — the question rides in the Executive's own reply — and the gate records `origin_session_id` plus the session's channel. Otherwise the question is delivered through `schedule_tools.handle_message_person`, which picks the person's preferred channel, falls through on a failed send, and falls back to a briefing alert; the gate then records the channel, address and provider message id that send returned, plus the id of the DM session it landed in — that send is always 1:1, so the answer belongs in that conversation and nowhere else. Without it the gate matched on person and channel alone, so an unrelated @mention in a public channel resolved it and had the acknowledgement, run title included, posted where everyone could read it. Delivery is not guaranteed: the outbound guard can suppress it (duplicate, rate cap, quiet hours) and an unreachable person gets the alert fallback. Both cases leave the routing fields empty and report `delivery` as `suppressed` / `alerted` rather than claiming someone was asked, and the chat tool's presentation hint changes accordingly.

**Matching a reply.** Each inbound adapter passes the message to `inbound_resolver.resolve_inbound_message` with its `session_id`. Matching is three-tier: an explicit `in_reply_to` against a stored `outbound_message_id`; otherwise a single open run on that channel; otherwise one utility-fast disambiguation call gated at 0.85 confidence. An unmatched explicit reference rules out only the candidates that carry a stored outbound id — the ones it could have matched — and the rest continue; rejecting outright meant an adapter that passes a thread id on every message (Slack's `thread_ts`) short-circuited the later tiers forever, and a global test let one delivered gate's id block an unrelated self-approval gate. Channel names are normalized (`slack_dm` ≡ `slack`), the delivered address is compared when both sides know it, a row whose `state_json` will not parse is refused (a corrupt row otherwise presents as a legacy one), and an empty stored channel is treated as a wildcard only for rows checkpointed before gate delivery existed. Two guards keep an open gate from swallowing unrelated traffic: a gate carrying an `origin_session_id` matches replies only from the conversations the adapter names (a Slack or Discord thread offers its parent channel session too, mirroring the history double-write, since a gate raised on a mention recorded that session while the answer arrives under the thread's — on Slack only when that person rooted the thread, or the alias would reach into a colleague's), and the parser can return `unrelated`, which declines to resolve and lets the message reach the normal chat path. The parser is handed the gate's own question, so a bare "yes" is judged against something. Its fallback is flagged by a key the model cannot emit rather than by a magic note string it could, and a fallback declines to resolve on *every* reply shape — recording the empty string a `free_text` fallback fabricates would close a sign-off on a parser outage. Every shape can answer `unrelated`, not just `approve_reject`: without it an open `free_text` gate turned the person's next message into its answer verbatim, and a `numeric` one swallowed any message containing a number. `resumer.apply_resolution` then records the decision, marks the run `resolved`, and writes an audit row. A timeout applies the step's `on_timeout` policy (escalate / auto_proceed / fail). The outcome surfaces on the Today dashboard.

**Resuming past the gate.** A paused run continues on its own. Re-entering it was long assumed to mean serializing a Python generator frame; it does not. The only state alive across a dynamic workflow's steps is its inputs (already persisted), a company-profile block that is recomputed, the completed steps' output strings, and the loop cursor — so the engine hands the checkpoint a small JSON `WorkflowResumeState` (workflow name, the gate's id and index, the next index, the outputs so far), stored in `workflow_runs.resume_state_json`, and `DynamicWorkflow.resume` replays its step loop from the recorded index. `run()` and `resume()` share that one loop, which is why a second gate needs no special handling — it is simply another pause raised from the same place. The payload rides on a `WaitForHumanEvent` field declared `exclude=True`, so it can never leak into `state_json`, whose exact key set the resolver branches on. A gate with no payload is *pause-only*: the decision is recorded and the run stops, which is what every caller got before resume existed.

`resumer._process_resumable` claims a resolved run with one guarded UPDATE — `resolved` → `running`, stamping `resumed_at` and minting a claim token — and drives it to a terminal row. It runs two ways: immediately, via a task `apply_resolution` kicks off so a Slack approval starts moving in seconds, and every 60s from the poll loop as the durable backstop. Both share the claim, so a run executes exactly once even with two resumers against one database. The poll runs the executor *after* the timeout loop, which is what finally makes `on_timeout='auto_proceed'` do what its name says: the timeout resolves the run and the same tick executes it. While the Executive is paused (`scheduler.pause`) the resumer does nothing — no startup sweep, no timeouts, no resumes — and `apply_resolution` still records the decision but skips the immediate kick; the first unpaused iteration catches up on all of it, so a timeout that lapsed during the pause applies its `on_timeout` policy then.

**The claim is fenced, because it is not a lease.** The stale sweep decides a worker is dead from a wall-clock guess, so a slow but *alive* worker will eventually be declared dead and replaced. Every write the executor makes carries its claim token and is refused once superseded — otherwise the replaced worker's late completion lands on top of its replacement's result, or its checkpoint at a later gate resurrects an already-finished run and asks the approver a second time. The retry budget resets at each new gate (a gate is new work, not a retry), and a run that exhausts it is *ended* rather than dropped: an exhausted run sits in `running` with a payload, in neither queue, and would otherwise show as in-progress forever.

**The gate fails closed.** Continuing is an allowlist — `approve` and the synthetic `auto_proceed` — not "anything that is not a stop word". `decision` is whatever a fast model extracted from free-form chat and it drifts; under a denylist, "rejected", "Reject", "decline" and "no" would all continue, so the approver declines and the deliverable is produced anyway. Reply shapes that ask a question rather than seek permission always continue, since the answer *is* the value. A stop ends the run at `error` with the human's note. Either way the decision becomes the gate step's own output, so it reads as a section *in* the artifact — capped and blockquoted, because that text reaches the synthesis specialist as prompt context.

**A definition edited during the pause is refused.** Resume re-validates the payload's version, the recorded gate, *and* a fingerprint of the whole step list, and derives the index to continue at rather than reading it from the payload. Pinning only the gate would not be enough: definitions are overwritten by name and any rostered user can save one, so someone could keep the gate identical and replace every step after it — and the approver's sign-off would be recorded against work they never saw, which defeats the one thing an approval gate is for. No built-in workflow yields the gate; only user-created dynamic workflows do.

### Launching from chat

Workflows are not only reachable from the `/jobs` UI — the Executive can list and run any of them mid-conversation. `openexecutive.orchestrator.workflow_run_tools` wires two tools into the main chat loop: `list_workflows` (the launchable catalog, with each workflow's input fields) and `run_workflow` (runs one to completion and returns its Markdown artifact, using the same engine as `POST /workflows/{name}/runs`). `run_workflow` resolves both built-ins and custom workflows via `get_workflow`, validates `inputs` against the workflow's input model, persists the run (`create_run` → `complete_run` / `fail_run`), and on an approval-gate step checkpoints the run as `awaiting_human` exactly as the HTTP route does — literally the same code, since both call `workflows.gate.checkpoint_gate`, which delivers the question and writes the checkpoint in one place. It never hangs waiting on a human, and it reports both whether the question reached them and whether the run will continue by itself once answered. The runners that *cannot* pause — the schedulers, evals, client rotation, onboarding, the research tools — call `gate.ensure_workflow_event`, which raises on a gate rather than letting one be swallowed; the scheduler's dynamic-workflow branch used to ignore it and record a successful run containing nothing. `executive_research` is excluded (it has the dedicated `run_executive_research` tool). Running a workflow from chat delivers nothing on its own — it renders the artifact into the conversation, and the recurring principal briefs (`morning_brief`, `end_of_day_digest`) reach anyone only via the scheduler's own `_deliver_to_principal`. The tool description used to claim those two DM the principal when run and to confirm before firing them, which had the model soliciting a confirmation on a false premise; it now names `executive_reflection` as the one workflow that really does execute tool calls of its own (DMs to heads, broadcasts, alerts). A successful run surfaces an `action_taken` chip linking to `/jobs/runs/{run_id}`.

### Dynamic (user-created) workflows

Users create reusable workflows on the fly — from the executive chat, the conversational wizard at `/jobs/new`, or the step-by-step advanced editor — without shipping code. A dynamic workflow is a stored JSON definition (the `dynamic_workflows` table) interpreted at runtime by one generic `DynamicWorkflow` engine (`openexecutive/workflows/dynamic.py`) that implements the same `Workflow` ABC as the built-ins, so the run path, SSE streaming, run persistence, and `/jobs/[name]` form rendering are unchanged. `get_workflow` / `list_workflows` fall through to the dynamic store after the static registry (built-ins win on a name collision).

A definition declares free-text input fields and an ordered step list of four kinds: **specialist** (consult a specialist with a goal prompt, optionally grounded by RAG), **action** (get something done with tools — see below), **approval_gate** (a `wait_for_human` pause), and a terminal **synthesis** step that assembles the artifact. At least one specialist or action step is required. `validate_definition` enforces the structural rules: exactly one terminal synthesis step, valid specialists, `{placeholder}` tokens that reference declared input fields, rostered approval/cadence people, and a parseable cadence.

Authoring from chat uses a **draft → confirm** handshake: the Executive calls `draft_workflow` (validate; return a `confirm_token` plus a plan summary), shows the user the plan, then calls `save_workflow` with the same definition and token — a token mismatch is rejected, so the saved workflow is exactly what the user approved. The step-by-step advanced editor drives the `/workflows/custom` CRUD endpoints directly.

**The New workflow wizard** (`/jobs/new`) is the default way to create one from the UI. It works like conversational onboarding: the user describes the job, the `workflow_designer` Council agent (`openexecutive/workflows/designer.py`) asks one clarifying question per turn — deliverable, per-run inputs, sign-off, schedule, recipient — with up to four clickable suggested answers, then emits a complete definition plus a plain-language summary and the assumptions it made. Every turn offers the model exactly three fixed, name-sorted tools (`ask_clarifying_question`, `emit_workflow_draft` — reusing the chat tool's `DEFINITION_SCHEMA` — and `search_available_tools`, which is answered inside the same turn from the tool catalog, up to four searches per turn, with the tool_use/tool_result pairs never stored in the plain-text transcript; every tool a search returns is remembered on the session and replayed into later turns, so a forced draft or a repair turn — which cannot search — still has the exact names); `tool_choice` flips to the emit tool once, when the six-question budget is spent or the user clicks *Draft it now*. The emitted definition goes through `validate_definition`, the tool-availability check, and a check against saved custom names, with one repair turn that feeds the errors back. The system prompt is a cached constant; the live context — specialists, the roster with person ids, the user's timezone (cadences are UTC), and taken names — is rendered once per session into the first user turn, and while refining, the exact current draft is prepended to the latest user turn so the model edits it rather than re-deriving it. Roster names and roles are flattened to one line and capped at 80 characters before they enter that context, and the system prompt tells the model to treat the whole block as data, never instructions. Sessions live in memory (`/workflows/designer/*`, 2 h TTL, 50-session cap), run one model turn at a time (a second concurrent `/message` or `/draft` gets 409, and a failed turn is rolled back by identity), and never write: the review card saves through the same `POST /workflows/custom`, which re-validates, and *Edit details* opens the draft in the advanced editor (`/jobs/new?designer=<id>`) before saving.

**Action steps (workflows that act).** An `action` step (`ActionStepSpec`: `goal`, `tools`, `max_tool_calls` 1–50, default 20) is run by the `workflow_actor` Council agent (`openexecutive/workflows/action_step.py`) as a bounded tool-use loop. Its `tools` list is an allowlist of exact tool names — MCP gateway tools (`server__tool`, e.g. `google_workspace__append_table_rows`) and a small set of built-ins (`oe__read_file`, `oe__message_person`, `oe__create_alert`) — and **clicking Create is the user's approval** of that list: the review card shows every tool, flags the ones that may change things (anything whose name doesn't say it reads, and any tool with a URL/URI/endpoint/webhook parameter anywhere in its schema, or whose schema couldn't be read, since a URL can carry data out), and names them in a "this workflow can use these without asking again" notice. Because that card is the approval, a workflow with action steps saved from chat (`draft_workflow`/`save_workflow`, whose confirmation is a token the model holds itself) is stored **switched off** (`is_active=false`) and `save_workflow` returns `status: saved_pending_review` with a `/jobs/{name}` link. An inactive workflow can't run or schedule (`get_workflow` and the scheduler skip it); `/jobs/{name}` shows it on the same review card, where **Turn on workflow** (`POST /workflows/custom/{name}/activate`, which re-validates the tools) is the approval — the click sends the definition the card showed, and the server refuses (409) if the stored one has changed since, so chat overwriting it while the card is open can't get new tools switched on. Chat may revise a switched-off workflow but refuses to replace a switched-on one that has action steps (an inbound email steering the Executive could otherwise switch off an approved job and stage new tools under its name); those edits happen in the advanced editor. The Workflows catalog (`/jobs`) lists switched-off workflows in a compact *Waiting for your approval* strip, and saving edits in the advanced editor keeps one off. `tool_catalog.py` resolves names to schemas through the gateway's `search_tools` (extensible-mcp's Markdown output is parsed; resolving is also the per-session discovery its `call_tool` requires) and validates availability at save time (`POST`/`PUT /workflows/custom`, chat `draft_workflow`/`save_workflow`, designer drafts) — an unknown, misspelled or deny-listed tool is a 422. The gateway meta-tools (`search_tools`, `call_tool`, `load_mcp_server`) can never be step tools. `run()` resolves every action step's tools before any step runs, so a vanished tool stops the run before an earlier step acts; `resume()` checks only the steps still to run, after the gate and decision are validated. The last turn of an action step always switches tools off so the agent can report. At run time only the allowlisted tools are offered (sorted; constant cached system block, per-run goal/inputs/earlier results in the user turn), every `tool_use` is re-checked against the allowlist, MCP calls go through `MCPGateway.call_tool` so the config deny-list and the Gmail/Calendar/Drive recipient gates still apply, the call budget is enforced (then a final tools-off turn asks for the report; running out of turns fails the step and lists what was already done), tool errors (the gateway's `Error:` / `Error calling tool` / `Tool error:` prefixes, or a truthy `error` field) return to the model as `is_error` results, each call emits a `progress` event and an audit row (`workflow_tool_call`: tool and outcome; for tools that may change things also a short digest of target arguments — ids, recipients, URLs, paths — so a redirected write is visible; content arguments are never logged), and the step's output is the agent's report plus an "Actions taken" list. Tool output is framed as data, never instructions.

**Targets are chosen at run time — and a new one is confirmed once.** Approving a workflow approves its *tools*; which sheet, doc, recipient or URL each call hits is chosen by the model at run time, by design (a tab per month, a reply to whoever sent the invoice, a doc per client). What bounds that is the allowlist, the gateway's recipient gates, the audit digest, and **first-write confirmation**: a `TargetPolicy` (one per run) checks every call to a tool that may change things. `resource_targets` walks its arguments recursively for resource keys (snake- or camel-case ids, `to`/`cc`/`bcc`, recipients, addresses, attendees, members, users, owners, parents, URLs/links/hrefs, paths, channels, spaces, rooms, phones, hosts, buckets, tables, spreadsheet/document/folder/calendar/file); a matching key marks everything beneath it, even a `name`. Outside a resource, only a new item's own `name`/`title`/`subject`, message/thread/draft/label ids, `range`/`sheet` and workspace-mcp's acting `user_google_email` are skipped — and whatever the key, a bare value shaped like an email address, a URL or an international phone number is a target, except inside what the call writes (`rows`, `values`, `body`, `text` …). Key names are a heuristic, so this is a best-effort guard layered on the allowlist, the gateway gates and the audit. Float ids are compared as integers. Arguments too deep, naming too many targets, or holding an over-long value **fail closed** (the call is refused). A target is trusted only when it was approved for this workflow before (`workflow_approved_targets`, by value) or is an id a write in this run created — a top-level id/link field (`id`, `spreadsheetId`, `webViewLink` …) of the **structured JSON object** result of a tool whose name says it creates (create / insert / upload …) and that takes no URL — a tool whose schema couldn't be read is assumed to (free text, nested records and readers' or updaters' results are never read, so a fetched page, an echoed title, a shared page's links or a stranger in `ccRecipients` can't plant one); those survive a pause in the resume payload (`run_created`). Values written in the workflow's own text are *not* trusted, since anyone who can edit the workflow could change them without review: they are asked once, then remembered. Approvals are by value, for any of the workflow's tools, and are **cleared when the workflow's tool set changes** (a newly added tool must earn them again). Any other target makes the call **held**: it is not run and costs no budget, the model is told it is waiting for approval and carries on, and it is audited `held for approval` (at most 10 held per step, 16 KB each; an identical repeat is held once). Whether a call is checked at all follows the read-only label, which now never marks a tool whose name carries a write verb anywhere (`find_and_replace_doc`). After the step finishes, the run pauses with a `WaitForHumanEvent` to the workflow's **owner** (`owner_person_id`, the person who created it on the Workflows page or in chat; falling back to the principal if unknown or archived), `on_timeout=auto_proceed`, 48 h, and a `WorkflowResumeState` of `kind="held_writes"` carrying the exact held calls. On resume (`_resume_held_writes`, fingerprint-checked like a gate, with the remaining steps' tools checked first), only `approve` runs them — each still has to be in the live step's allowlist and resolve; its targets are remembered first — and anything else (decline, timeout, unreadable) skips them; either way a *Held for approval* section is added to the step's output and the run continues at the next step. With no one to ask, held writes are skipped and noted; a step that fails or crashes after holding, or a resume that stops early (definition changed, a later tool missing), audits its held writes as dropped and says they did not run. The question quotes each target JSON-escaped (a value can't add its own lines) and always shows a URL's full scheme and host, saying how much of the rest is hidden. The owner answers by chat reply or with **Approve / Decline** on the run page (`POST /workflows/runs/{id}/decision`, which the principal may also use); remembered targets are listed and removable on the workflow page.

`oe__read_file` extracts text (PDF, Word, Excel, CSV, Markdown, text) only from files under `WORKFLOW_FILE_DIRS` (default: workspace-mcp's attachment folder), resolving symlinks and `..` before the check. Action steps are allowed in scheduled workflows. Because they have external side effects, a resumed run heartbeats its claim (`touch_resume_claim`, at most once a minute as events flow — each tool call emits one; a busy database is retried on the next heartbeat, never treated as a lost claim; the sweep's requeue re-checks the claim's age in the same UPDATE, so a heartbeat landing between the sweep's read and its write wins), so the stale-claim sweep never requeues and replays a slow but live run, and a worker that finds its claim superseded stops at its next event. A worker that actually crashes mid-resume is still requeued; its action steps then run again, so goals should say how to avoid duplicates (the actor reads current state before writing). `GET /workflows/tools/search?q=` and `GET /workflows/tools/describe?names=` back the advanced editor's tool picker and the review card's labels.

An optional cadence (`daily@` / `weekly@` / `quarterly@`) re-uses the scheduler via the `dynamic_workflow` action kind, which runs the workflow on schedule and DMs the artifact to a rostered recipient. A gate followed by further steps pauses at `awaiting_human` and then resumes once answered, so gates no longer have to sit immediately before synthesis. They remain forbidden in cadence-enabled definitions: a scheduled fire has no interactive human to ask.

Built-ins the system runs on its own (`morning_brief`, `end_of_day_digest`, `executive_reflection`, `executive_research`) set `background = True`, surfaced as `WorkflowMeta.background`; the `/jobs` catalog files them under a **System** chip instead of the default view. They stay runnable by hand.

**Workflows vs. playbooks.** `/jobs` has three tabs: **Catalog**, **Runs**, and **Playbooks** (`?tab=playbooks`; `/skills` redirects there). A playbook is a skill (`knowledge/skills_repo.py`): *how* the Executive does a piece of work, with no inputs, schedule or side effects. A workflow is the runnable job. Workflows **follow** playbooks: a step that follows one gets its body appended to the step prompt via `workflows/playbooks.py` (`load_playbook` + `playbook_clause`). Six built-ins do — `board_prep` (`board-prep-deck`), `quarterly_plan` (`quarterly-okr-set`, `quarterly-forecast`), `mbr` (`monthly-business-review`, in the financial, KPI and function steps), `competitive_teardown` (`competitive-teardown`, in the four analysis steps), `fundraising_prep` (`fundraise-narrative`, narrative step) and `exec_search_brief` (`role-scorecard`, profile step). Each declares them in `Workflow.playbooks`; a unit test holds that declaration equal to the `load_playbook("…")` calls in the module, and `WorkflowMeta.playbooks` exposes it. A custom workflow's `specialist` step may name a `playbook` (validated to exist at save; appended after `{field}` rendering, so braces in a playbook are never treated as placeholders). The lookup resolves the playbook in effect, so a company's customized copy changes the workflow's output, and a hidden, missing or malformed one falls back to the step's own prompt plus RAG — a workflow never fails over a playbook (`load_playbook` catches everything; a custom step whose playbook is unavailable emits a `progress` event saying so). Because an approved scheduled workflow reads its playbook at each run, the chat tools refuse to edit or delete any playbook a workflow follows, or to create one under a name a workflow still follows after its playbook was deleted; if the workflow list can't be read they refuse (`unverifiable`) rather than assume nothing follows it. Only a person on the Playbooks tab can change what a workflow follows, and the chat summary of a drafted workflow names each step's playbook. `playbook_users()` maps each playbook to the workflows that follow it — built-ins and every custom workflow, switched-off ones included (turning one on approves its definition, so what it follows must not have changed from chat meanwhile); the skills API reports it as `used_by`, and the Executive's `search_skills` hits carry it as `workflows`.

Completed artifacts are discoverable in the unified Artifacts section (`/artifacts`) alongside their run-detail page at `/jobs/runs/{run_id}`.

## Data-driven retrospectives

`engagement_value_report` introduces a new workflow pattern: instead of the user typing the substance into a form (the `investor_update` / `mbr` shape), the workflow **reads its substance from the database**. A deterministic gatherer (`clients/engagement_activity.py`) pulls the period's decisions, initiatives, advisory consultations, delivered workflow artifacts (excluding prior value reports), follow-through counts, and alerts handled — from the live DB for the active client, or a parked client slot's `state.db` opened read-only. A single board-comms call narrates those facts (the prompt forbids inventing anything not in them; an empty period skips the LLM entirely), and the artifact's lists are assembled deterministically. Built for renewal conversations — the engagement record is the evidence.
